newsitem.title: USA: Greens sue for Nader to join election debates.
newsitem.headline: Greens sue for Nader to join election debates.

text.p: The Green Party filed a lawsuit Friday demanding that presidential candidate Ralph Nader be included in debates that election authorities have restricted to the two major political parties.

The lawsuit sought a temporary restraining order against the Commission on Presidential Debates from enforcing rules that excluded consumer advocate Nader, Ross Perot of the Reform Party and John Hagelin of the Natural Law Party.
The lawsuit, which also names the Federal Election Commission as a defendant, was expected to be heard Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Washington.

"These debates are a chance for all of us to put our respective candidates in there so that the American public can hear what he has to say...and make a determination as citizens of a country that is supposedly a democracy and has flaunted the democratic process," said plaintiff Craig Seeman, a New York state assembly Green Party candidate from Brooklyn.
The Green Party said Nader was on the ballot in 21 states and the District of Columbia and had qualified in states casting 225 electoral votes.

Attorneys for the party said the lawsuit was different from those filed by Perot and Hagelin because it raised constitutional issues of citizens' rights to a free election, including access to an open forum.

But like the lawsuit filed by Texas billionaire Perot, it challenged the debate commission's argument that minority candidates be excluded on the grounds that they have no reasonable chance of being elected.

Negotiators for President Bill Clinton and Republican candidate Bob Dole agreed to hold two one-on-one televised debates between their candidates on Oct 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, and Oct. 16 in San Diego. A vice presidential debate was scheduled for Oct. 9 in St. Petersburg, Florida.
